subject: english-language
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Analysing language, structure and their effects

questions.q: What is the title of Paper 2 (Component 02) in the OCR GCSE (9–1) English Language specification?
options: Communicating information and ideas
Exploring effects and impact
Exploring poetry and drama
Analysing spoken language
questions.explain: OCR Component 02 is titled 'Exploring effects and impact' and focuses on fiction and literary non-fiction.

questions.q: Which of these best describes what Assessment Objective 2 (AO2) requires?
options: Identify and interpret explicit and implicit information
Analyse how writers use language and structure to achieve effects and influence readers
Compare writers' ideas and perspectives across texts
Communicate clearly and imaginatively in your own writing
questions.explain: AO2 assesses analysis of how writers' language and structural choices create effects, using subject terminology.

questions.q: What does Assessment Objective 3 (AO3) require candidates to do?
options: Evaluate a single text critically
Compare writers' ideas and perspectives, and how these are conveyed, across two or more texts
Write a persuasive article for a set audience
Correct spelling, punctuation and grammar
questions.explain: AO3 is the comparison objective, requiring candidates to link ideas and methods across texts.

questions.q: A simile is a comparison that does which of the following?
options: States that one thing actually is another
Compares two things using 'like' or 'as'
Gives human qualities to non-human things
Repeats a consonant sound at the start of words
questions.explain: A simile compares two things explicitly using 'like' or 'as', for example 'as cold as ice'.

questions.q: Which statement correctly defines a metaphor?
options: A comparison stating that one thing is another, without 'like' or 'as'
A word that imitates a sound
An exaggeration for effect
A phrase whose meaning is not literal but idiomatic
questions.explain: A metaphor directly states one thing is another, e.g. 'the classroom was a zoo'.

questions.q: What is personification?
options: Comparing two things using 'as'
Giving human qualities or actions to something non-human
Deliberate exaggeration for emphasis
The repetition of vowel sounds
questions.explain: Personification attributes human characteristics to objects, animals or ideas, e.g. 'the fire danced'.

questions.q: What types of text are read in the reading section of OCR Paper 2?
options: Two non-fiction information leaflets
One literary fiction text and one literary non-fiction text
A Shakespeare play and a modern poem
Two texts from a poetry anthology
questions.explain: Paper 2 pairs literary fiction with literary non-fiction so candidates explore effects and impact across both.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes what Assessment Objective 5 (AO5) assesses in the writing task?
options: Accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar
The ability to communicate clearly, effectively and imaginatively, and organise ideas
Comparing perspectives across two texts
Interpreting implicit information
questions.explain: AO5 rewards clear, imaginative communication and effective organisation of content and ideas.

questions.q: A writer uses a series of short, blunt sentences during an action scene. What effect is this most likely to create?
options: A calm, reflective and leisurely mood
A sense of pace, tension or urgency
A formal, academic tone
Confusion about the setting
questions.explain: Short sentences quicken the pace and build tension, mirroring fast or dramatic action.

questions.q: Why might a writer choose a first-person narrative voice in a piece of fiction?
options: To hide the narrator's feelings from the reader
To create intimacy and give direct insight into the narrator's thoughts and feelings
To present an objective, unbiased account
To describe several characters equally
questions.explain: First-person narration draws the reader close, offering direct access to one character's perspective and emotions.

questions.q: What is the effect of a writer building a semantic field of words linked to darkness and decay?
options: It creates a light-hearted, comic tone
It establishes a consistent mood or atmosphere, such as menace or gloom
It confuses the reader deliberately
It signals the end of the text
questions.explain: A semantic field is a cluster of related words that reinforces a particular mood, theme or atmosphere.

questions.q: When a question asks about 'implicit' meaning, what does it want you to do?
options: Quote information that is stated directly
Infer meaning that is suggested but not stated outright
Count how many times a word appears
Summarise the whole text
questions.explain: Implicit meaning is implied between the lines, so it must be inferred rather than lifted directly.

questions.q: A writer describes storm clouds gathering just as a character receives bad news. This use of pathetic fallacy is most likely intended to do what?
options: Provide an accurate weather report
Reflect or foreshadow the character's emotions or events
Introduce a new setting for comic effect
Slow the pace with technical detail
questions.explain: Pathetic fallacy uses weather or nature to mirror mood or hint at events to come.

questions.q: Which feature is most characteristic of a strong comparative (AO3) response?
options: A full summary of Text A followed by a full summary of Text B
Integrated points that link both texts and analyse how their ideas are conveyed
A personal opinion on which text is more enjoyable
A list of quotations with no analysis
questions.explain: Effective comparison weaves both texts together, analysing similarities and differences in ideas and methods.

questions.q: In descriptive writing, why is sensory language (sight, sound, smell, touch, taste) effective?
options: It makes the writing shorter
It immerses the reader by appealing to the senses and creating vivid imagery
It removes the need for punctuation
It guarantees a factual, objective tone
questions.explain: Sensory detail brings a scene to life, helping the reader experience it and increasing impact.

questions.q: A text ends by echoing the image it opened with. What is the effect of this cyclical structure?
options: It creates a sense of completeness or that nothing has changed
It suddenly shifts the setting
It signals an unreliable narrator
It removes tension from the ending
questions.explain: A cyclical structure returns to the opening, suggesting resolution, entrapment or that events have come full circle.

questions.q: Which device is used in the sentence: 'The wind screamed through the broken window and clawed at the curtains'?
options: Simile
Personification
Onomatopoeia
Hyperbole
questions.explain: The wind is given human actions ('screamed', 'clawed'), which is personification.

questions.q: A creative writing task asks you to describe a busy market. Which opening is most likely to achieve strong effect and impact?
options: A dictionary-style definition of the word 'market'
A vivid sensory image placing the reader amid the sounds and smells of the stalls
A chronological account beginning 'First, I got up and had breakfast.'
A list of facts about local trade
questions.explain: An immediate sensory image engages the reader and demonstrates imaginative, effective writing (AO5).

questions.q: Text A presents the sea as terrifying and hostile; Text B presents it as peaceful and healing. Which is the strongest comparative point?
options: Text A describes waves crashing on rocks in the storm
Both writers convey contrasting attitudes to the sea: A uses violent verbs to make it hostile, whereas B uses gentle imagery to make it calming
The sea is a large body of salt water in both texts
Text B is more enjoyable to read than Text A
questions.explain: A strong AO3 point links both texts and compares how their methods convey contrasting perspectives.

questions.q: In the line 'She clutched the letter, her hands trembling as she forced herself to read the first line', what can most reasonably be inferred about the character?
options: She is bored and indifferent
She is anxious or fearful about the letter's contents
She is celebrating good news
She cannot read
questions.explain: Details such as 'trembling' and 'forced herself' imply fear or anxiety, an inference rather than a stated fact.

specSource: OCR GCSE (9–1) English Language (J351) specification; Paper 2: Exploring Effects and Impact
